questions.question_description: Implement a Singly Linked List with operations to Insert at End and Delete at End. After multiple operations, display the final list.
questions.input_format: Integer N (number of operations), followed by N lines of commands: 'ins_end X' (insert value X), 'del_end' (delete last element), 'display' (print list).
questions.output_format: For 'display', print space-separated elements. Print 'Empty' if the list is empty. For 'del_end' on an empty list, print 'Underflow'.
questions.constraints: 1 <= N <= 1000. Data values fit in standard integer.
questions.hints: Maintain a head pointer. Insert at end requires traversing to the last node. Delete at end requires traversing to the second-to-last node and freeing the last node.

test_cases.input:
6
ins_end 1
ins_end 2
del_end
ins_end 3
ins_end 4
display

questions.solution_explanation: Singly Linked List allows dynamic sizing. Inserting at the end is O(N) when only a head pointer is maintained since we traverse to the last element. Deleting the last node is also O(N) as we need to find the second-to-last node to sever the link.

questions.question_description: Implement a Doubly Linked List supporting insertion at end, deletion at end, forward display, and reverse display. The nodes must have prev and next pointers.
questions.input_format: Integer N (number of operations), followed by N lines of commands: 'ins_end X' (insert value X), 'del_end' (delete last), 'display' (print forward), 'display_rev' (print reverse).
questions.output_format: Print elements space-separated for display commands. Print 'Empty' if the list contains 0 elements. Print 'Underflow' on an invalid delete operation.
questions.hints: A doubly linked list node has 'prev' and 'next' pointers. Maintain a tail pointer alongside your head pointer for O(1) insertions at the end and O(1) reverse traversals.

test_cases.input:
6
ins_end 1
ins_end 2
ins_end 3
del_end
display
display_rev

7
ins_end 4
ins_end 5
ins_end 6
del_end
ins_end 7
display
display_rev

questions.solution_explanation: Doubly Linked List allows transversal in both directions. Maintaining both a head and a tail pointer makes appending an element, deleting the last element, and printing backward all O(1) initial overhead operations without requiring traversal.

questions.question_description: Given two sorted singly linked lists, merge them together into a single sorted singly linked list and print the result. The merged list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists in sorted order.
questions.input_format: Integer N followed by N sorted elements for the first list. Integer M followed by M sorted elements for the second list.
questions.output_format: Space-separated elements of the merged sorted list. If both lists are empty, print 'Empty'.
questions.hints: Maintain pointers traversing along both linked lists. Compare the current nodes and append the smaller value to your new result linked list recursively or iteratively.
questions.solution_explanation: Merging requires O(N + M) time. We iterate through both linked lists simultaneously, comparing the current values and pulling the minimal node into the result list. Finally, we append any remaining leftover nodes.

questions.question_description: Implement polynomial addition using singly linked lists. Two polynomials are provided exactly in descending order of their exponents. Each node contains a coefficient and an exponent. Add both polynomials and output the resulting polynomial terms in descending order. Exclude any terms with a coefficient of 0.
questions.input_format: Integer N (terms for Polynomial 1) followed by N space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs. Then Integer M (terms for Polynomial 2) followed by M space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs.
questions.output_format: Print the combined polynomial as space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs. If the final sum polynomial is essentially zero, print '0 0'.
questions.constraints: 0 <= N, M <= 100. Exponents are non-negative integers strictly formatted in decreasing order.
questions.hints: Treat this similar to merging two sorted lists. Traverse both lists; if one exponent is greater, attach it to result. If equal, add coefficients and attach the combined term (only if coefficient != 0).
questions.solution_explanation: Polynomials use linked list nodes storing coefficient and exponent. The addition is performed by merging two exponentially descending lists: if exponents equalize, coefficients are summed and preserved only if non-zero. Otherwise, the term with a larger exponent takes precedence.

questions.question_description: Implement polynomial multiplication using singly linked lists. Two polynomials are provided exactly in descending order of their exponents. Each node contains a coefficient and an exponent. Multiply both polynomials and output the resulting polynomial terms in descending order. Exclude any terms with a coefficient of 0.
questions.input_format: Integer N (terms for Polynomial 1) followed by N space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs. Then Integer M (terms for Polynomial 2) followed by M space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs.
questions.output_format: Print the combined multiplied polynomial as space-separated <coefficient> <exponent> pairs in descending order. If the final sum polynomial is essentially zero, print '0 0'.
questions.constraints: 0 <= N, M <= 100. Exponents are non-negative integers formatted in decreasing order.
questions.hints: Multiply every term in polynomial 1 with every term in polynomial 2. Create a new linked list and insert the product terms (coefficient1 * coefficient2, exponent1 + exponent2). If a term with the same exponent already exists in the result list, add the coefficients together.
questions.solution_explanation: Polynomial multiplication is achieved by cross-multiplying every node in the first list with every node in the second list. The coefficients are multiplied, and the exponents are added. Each resulting term is inserted into a new result linked list while maintaining descending exponent order and combining (adding coefficients) any terms with matching exponents.
